section_summaries.epidemiology: Buruli ulcer, caused by Mycobacterium ulcerans, is a neglected tropical disease with high focal prevalence mainly within rural West and Central Africa, affecting children and young adults, but also found in over 30 countries globally including temperate Australia, where it affects elderly residents. Transmission mode is unknown, though M. ulcerans has been identified in wild animals, and water bugs are implicated as potential vectors. Disturbance of water systems, newly arrived migrants, and specific ecological niches (slow-flowing/stagnant water) are associated with increased incidence.
section_summaries.pathogenesis: The extensive tissue destruction and subcutaneous necrosis characteristic of Buruli ulcer are caused by mycolactone, a lipid toxin secreted by Mycobacterium ulcerans. This plasmid-encoded polyketide molecule is cytotoxic and also prevents the development of an inflammatory response, which is a unique pathogenic mechanism among mycobacteria.
section_summaries.clinical_manifestations: Patients typically present with a chronic, painless ulcer of several months' duration. Early lesions may appear as a 1-5 cm painless subcutaneous nodule or papular. More extensive indurated plaques and edema may also occur. Ulceration spreads from the initial lesion, with distinguishing features including painless undermined edges. In 90% of cases, ulcers involve the limbs, but can affect any part of the body, leading to disfiguring scars, limited joint movement, and occasionally osteomyelitis; systemic symptoms like fever are rare unless secondary bacterial infection occurs.
section_summaries.diagnosis: Diagnosis is primarily clinical, though distinguishing from diabetic or venous stasis ulcers can be challenging. Acid-fast bacilli can be detected in 40% of ulcers by swab. Cultures on Löwenstein-Jensen medium (32°C) are more sensitive (up to 60%) but take 6+ weeks. Histologic examination is 85% sensitive but often unavailable. The most sensitive diagnostic test (98%) is PCR for the IS2404 repeat sequence of M. ulcerans, applicable to swabs, punch biopsies, and fine needle aspirates.
section_summaries.treatment: Treatment involves 8 weeks of daily rifampin (10 mg/kg orally, max 600 mg) and clarithromycin (15 mg/kg orally, or 500 mg orally twice a day if not extended release). Streptomycin was previously used but is no longer routinely available. Fluoroquinolone antibiotics also show some activity. Most lesions heal without surgery, but large ulcers may require debridement and split-skin grafting. Standard dressing involves gauze coated with Vaseline changed daily. Early treatment prevents disabilities.
section_summaries.prevention: Preventing M. ulcerans infection requires understanding its transmission to humans, which is currently unknown. Exposure to water sources in endemic areas is a risk factor, but reducing this exposure, especially for children, is impractical. There is no effective vaccine, though BCG provides short-lived protection in some trials. Outreach programs to educate communities about early lesion recognition are crucial for preventing severe disease forms.
